clue.text: The engineer's an absolutely essential fellow

definitions.text: The engineer's an absolutely essential fellow

parts.words: The engineer's an absolutely essential fellow
parts.note: a ship's engineer who tends the small auxiliary engine, described as a fellow who is utterly vital: a university fellow (don) plus a key man

explanation.surface: Praise for an engineer as the one person nobody can do without.
explanation.walkthrough: The description hides its own pieces: a fellow (DON), and 'absolutely essential fellow' is a KEY MAN, and together they name the seaman who works the ship's auxiliary engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey engine is a small auxiliary engine on a ship, and the crewman who works it is named after it.

clue.text: Radical support, often quoted, for the honour of knighthood

annotationWithheld.why: Radical support, often quoted, for the honour of knighthood (9): no parse found for the given answer; 'Radical support, often quoted' gives no letters I can account for
annotationWithheld.clue: Radical support, often quoted, for the honour of knighthood

clue.text: Initial service organisation

parts.note: a body serving the armed forces whose name is known by its initial letters

explanation.surface: The body that first provided a service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initial' looks like 'first'; it means the organisation is known by its initials: the Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes, which run canteens for British service personnel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes run shops and canteens for the British military, and are always known by their initials.

clue.text: Presented at court, out of a box

definitions.text: Presented at court, out of a box

parts.words: Presented at court, out of a box
parts.note: testimony given by someone standing in the witness box during a trial

explanation.surface: Something unpacked and shown off at a royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presented at court' suggests a debutante before the monarch; the court is a law court and the box the witness box.
explanation.definitionFit: What a witness states in the box is testimony offered to prove the facts of a case.

clue.text: Chaucer's story-teller supplies learned society

parts.note: one of the Canterbury pilgrims, by trade the officer who buys provisions for a college or inn of court

explanation.surface: A narrator from the Canterbury Tales provides an academic body with something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supplies' looks like a verb with 'learned society' as its object; it describes the pilgrim's job, buying food for a college or Inn of Court.
explanation.definitionFit: Among the Canterbury pilgrims is the purchasing steward of an Inn of Court, who tells a tale; such stewards also served colleges.

clue.text: A pure beginner

parts.note: a complete learner, and also a probationer entering a religious order, pure in life

explanation.surface: Someone who is starting out from absolute scratch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pure' means 'utter' in the surface, but also suggests the chastity of a new entrant to a convent.
explanation.definitionFit: A probationary member of a religious community is the term also used for any inexperienced learner.

clue.text: Piece of equipment for public hanging

definitions.text: Piece of equipment for public hanging

parts.words: Piece of equipment for public hanging
parts.note: not the gallows but the loop that standing passengers hang on to in a bus or train

explanation.surface: An item of kit used at an execution in front of a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Public hanging' suggests the gallows; the public here are standing passengers on public transport, hanging from loops.
explanation.definitionFit: Buses and underground trains have leather loops overhead that standing passengers grip.

clue.text: 29's heroine acts so winningly!

parts.note: the heroine of the comedy by the playwright at 29, who pretends to be a barmaid in order to win her man, as the play's title says

explanation.surface: An actress from a play gives a charming performance.
explanation.walkthrough: The play by the dramatist at 29 is 'She Stoops to Conquer': its heroine, Kate Hardcastle, lowers herself to win, so she 'acts so' (stooping) to conquer.
explanation.definitionFit: Kate Hardcastle bends low in social rank to conquer, and bending low is crouching or lowering oneself.

clue.text: That's obviously another issue

parts.note: not a change of subject but a fresh printing of a book, which is plainly a further publication

explanation.surface: A speaker dismissing a point as a different matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another issue' sounds like 'a separate problem'; an issue is also a publication, and a new edition of a book is another one.
explanation.definitionFit: A book brought out again in a fresh version is a second or later printing.

clue.text: What's the point of rock-climbing ?

parts.note: not a question about the sport's purpose but the metal spike a climber hammers into rock

explanation.surface: A sceptic asking why anyone bothers to climb cliffs.
explanation.walkthrough: The question reads as 'why climb at all?'; the point meant is a literal one, the metal peg driven into a crack.
explanation.definitionFit: Climbers drive a metal peg with an eye into a crack in the rock to anchor a rope.

clue.text: It should be kept in the main for exercise

definitions.text: It should be kept in the main for exercise

parts.words: It should be kept in the main for exercise
parts.note: the main is the open sea, and a warship on naval exercises must hold its assigned position in the fleet

explanation.surface: Something that ought mostly to be maintained for the sake of physical fitness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' looks like 'mostly' and 'exercise' like a workout; the main is the high sea and the exercise a naval one, where ships keep their positions.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships in formation 'keep station', holding a fixed place relative to the others.

clue.text: Unrestrainedly forceful novel, it seems

indicators.note: the letters only seem to be the words novel and it; really they are these words in disguise, rearranged

explanation.surface: A book that appears to be wildly aggressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seems' says the words are only an appearance: the letters of NOVEL and IT rearrange to give the answer. 'Novel' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done with wild, uncontrolled force is aggressive in the extreme.

clue.text: Popeye's immortal bird is not born for death, it seems

definitions.text: Popeye's immortal bird is not born for death, it seems

parts.words: Popeye's immortal bird is not born for death, it seems
parts.note: the cartoon sailor's girlfriend (bird is slang for girl), a character who never ages, whose name reads as '...!'

explanation.surface: The cartoon sailor's undying sweetheart was apparently never meant to die.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is British slang for a young woman, so Popeye's bird is his sweetheart, Olive Oyl. Her name split as 'O LIVE' is a cry to live, fit for someone not born for death.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Popeye cartoons, the sailor's long-standing girlfriend is Olive Oyl, a comic character who has never grown old.

clue.text: A nice point for a start

indicators.note: the words nice and point are given in exchange for, that is turned into, a new arrangement of their letters

explanation.surface: A good argument to open a discussion with.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of NICE and POINT, nine in all, rearrange to give the answer; 'for' is the only word signalling the change, and 'a start' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The beginning or founding of an enterprise is its commencement.

clue.text: What there is to show for little work

definitions.text: What there is to show for little work

parts.words: What there is to show for little work
parts.note: not the meagre result of idleness but a literal name for a small piece of writing or music

explanation.surface: The poor result of hardly any effort.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds like a complaint about laziness; read literally, a 'little work' is a minor composition, which is what the word means.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin opus, a work, with a diminutive ending: a minor literary or musical composition.

clue.text: Beasts of devilish legend ?

parts.note: animals with hoofs, as the devil is said to have cloven ones

explanation.surface: Monsters from a fiendish folk tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Devilish legend' suggests monsters; legend says the devil has cloven hoofs, and the beasts meant are all hoofed mammals.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoofed mammals such as cattle, deer and horses form this zoological group, and the devil is pictured with hoofs.

clue.text: Have the figures at your fingertips, and use them

definitions.text: Have the figures at your fingertips, and use them

parts.words: Have the figures at your fingertips, and use them
parts.note: the numbered face of an old rotary telephone, worked by turning it with a finger, and the act of doing so

explanation.surface: Advice to know the statistics thoroughly and put them to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At your fingertips' means 'known thoroughly', but here the figures are literally under your fingers on a telephone, and using them is making a call.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotary telephone has a numbered disc that is turned with a finger to place a call, and that action has the same name.

clue.text: In which it could be fatal to lose one's thread

definitions.text: In which it could be fatal to lose one's thread

parts.words: In which it could be fatal to lose one's thread
parts.note: the Minotaur's maze in Crete, from which Theseus escaped by following a ball of thread

explanation.surface: A situation in which losing the drift of an argument would be disastrous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose one's thread' means forget what you were saying; in the Greek myth Theseus unwound Ariadne's thread to find his way out of the Minotaur's maze.
explanation.definitionFit: A maze of winding passages, like the one built for the Minotaur, is easy to get lost in.

clue.text: It's a capital arrangement, but it would be wrong to play on it

definitions.text: It's a capital arrangement, but it would be wrong to play on it

parts.words: It's a capital arrangement, but it would be wrong to play on it
parts.note: a hairstyle on the head (capital, from Latin caput), with a nod to the game of pinning a tail on a donkey

explanation.surface: An excellent plan that nobody should exploit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' means 'excellent' in the surface but 'of the head' here: a hairstyle. The party game pins a tail on a drawn donkey, so pinning one on a hairstyle would be wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair drawn back and tied at the back of the head hangs like a small horse's tail.

clue.text: Where people with studious interests draw together

definitions.text: Where people with studious interests draw together

parts.words: Where people with studious interests draw together
parts.note: a lesson in which students sketch side by side, studies being drawings

explanation.surface: A place where scholarly people gather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw together' suggests coming together; here people literally draw together, and 'studious' plays on studies, which are sketches.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesson in drawing or painting gathers students who sketch together.

clue.text: Passion's in fashion

definitions.meaning: 'all the' fury means popular, the craze of the moment

explanation.surface: Ardour is now the trendy thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A fit of fury is a violent passion, and something that is 'all the' craze is fashionable.

clue.text: It gives access to the Turners

definitions.text: It gives access to the Turners

parts.words: It gives access to the Turners
parts.note: not a gallery of the painter's works but the handle that people turn to open a door

explanation.surface: A ticket or entrance to the gallery of J. M. W. Turner's paintings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Turners' suggests the painter's canvases at the Tate; the turners are simply whoever turns the handle to get through a door.
explanation.definitionFit: A round handle is twisted to release the latch so that a door can be opened.

clue.text: The betting impulse is widespread and growing

parts.note: SP stands for starting price, the odds on a horse at the start of a race
an urge is a sudden impulse

explanation.surface: Gambling fever is everywhere and on the increase.
explanation.walkthrough: SP is the bookmaker's abbreviation for starting price, the odds at the off. The definition describes a plant: a common weed that grows everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a family of weeds with milky sap, found growing almost everywhere.

clue.text: Chinese chow ?

parts.note: a chow is a Chinese breed of dog, and chow is also slang for food, so the phrase suggests a hot snack

explanation.surface: A request for Chinese food.
explanation.walkthrough: Chow is slang for food and also a Chinese breed of dog, so a dog that is food is the snack of a sausage in a bun.
explanation.definitionFit: A frankfurter in a bread roll is fast food, and a chow is a canine breed from China.

clue.text: Counterpoint that ends on a false note

definitions.text: Counterpoint that ends on a false note

parts.words: Counterpoint that ends on a false note
parts.note: music of many independent voices, whose name happens to finish with a word meaning fake

explanation.surface: A piece of contrapuntal music that closes with a wrong note.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for counterpoint does literally end on 'false': its last five letters spell PHONY.
explanation.definitionFit: Music combining several independent melodic lines at once is contrapuntal by nature.

clue.text: Pointless woman's work

parts.note: a kind of fine needlework, traditionally done by women, with its final word removed

explanation.surface: A dismissive view of housework as futile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointless' looks like 'futile'; it means the word 'point' is dropped from petit point, a fine embroidery stitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Petit point is fine tent-stitch embroidery; taking off its second word leaves the French for small.

clue.text: What one professes to obtain in academic life

definitions.text: What one professes to obtain in academic life

parts.words: What one professes to obtain in academic life
parts.note: the post a professor holds, the title being punned on 'professes'

explanation.surface: The claimed ambition of a university career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Professes' looks like 'claims'; it means 'becomes a professor', and a professorship is called by the name of a seat.
explanation.definitionFit: A university professorship is named after the seat of office, as in 'the chair of history'.

clue.text: It. provides one with bail, and in due course acquittal

definitions.text: It. provides one with bail, and in due course acquittal

indicators.note: the letters of one and bail are supplied in a rearranged form

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: An excuse that gets a defendant out on bail and later cleared.
explanation.walkthrough: I (one) with the letters of BAIL rearranged gives the answer, and the whole clue describes what a good defence of being elsewhere does: release now, acquittal later.
explanation.definitionFit: Proof of being elsewhere at the time of a crime gets a suspect freed and finally cleared.

clue.text: Taught to express friendliness to a French communist ?

parts.note: the French address a friend with the familiar 'tu' rather than the formal 'vous'
taken as written
red is the usual crossword word for a communist

explanation.surface: Instructed in how to greet a French comrade warmly.
explanation.walkthrough: Speaking to a Frenchman, you show friendliness by calling him 'tu', which gives TU; then TO as written and RED for the communist.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil who has been given private lessons has been instructed by a teacher.

clue.text: An ARIBA engaged to make a start on multi-storied work ?

indicators.note: the letters of these words are set to work, employed in a new order

parts.note: taken as written: the letters after an Associate of the Royal Institute of British Architects

explanation.surface: An architect is hired to begin a tall building.
explanation.walkthrough: An ARIBA is a qualified British architect, so 'multi-storied' suggests a tower block; the work is the Arabian Nights, full of stories, and the answer is its first word. 'Engaged' turns AN ARIBA into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The collection of tales told by Scheherazade is usually titled the Arabian Nights, so this word opens its name.

clue.text: Discrepancies, in, this sense, don't affect the book-keeping

definitions.text: Discrepancies, in, this sense, don't affect the book-keeping

parts.words: Discrepancies, in, this sense, don't affect the book-keeping
parts.note: the saying that there is no accounting for personal preference, read as if about accountants

explanation.surface: Errors of this kind don't upset the accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says there is no accounting for one's sense of what is pleasing, so differences in it leave the accounts untouched.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the five senses, and also a person's judgment of what is pleasing, as in the proverb about accounting.

clue.text: Playwright wiht his own company

parts.note: an eighteenth-century Irish dramatist whose surname is shared by a London livery company of metalworkers

explanation.surface: A dramatist who runs his own theatre troupe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' suggests a troupe of actors; it is one of the City of London livery companies, the Worshipful Company of workers in gold, whose trade name is the dramatist's surname. 'Wiht' is the paper's misprint for 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver, author of the comedy about a mistaken inn, bears the surname of a craftsman in precious metal, and the City guild of such craftsmen is a livery company.
